comparedAgainst: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie -- thorough on definitions but diagram-light (one static, unthemed tree image with no compressed-trie/radix figure at all), no runnable code, no measured memory or timing data, nothing tuned for a 390px viewport.

https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/trie-insert-and-search/ -- ad-dense reference page, static raster diagrams that do not adapt to dark mode, array-of-26-children C/Java/Python snippets with no benchmark against any alternative structure and no honest discussion of when a trie loses.

https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/52trie/ -- Sedgewick & Wayne's own companion page (also cited as a source here): solid textbook coverage and real code, but no dark theme, no phone-width tuning, no measured trie-vs-sorted-array comparison and no compressed-trie figure; this article's Figure 2 and the 500-to-200,000-word benchmark go further than the source it draws on.
justification: Real numbers from my own serial `node tools/verify-page.mjs --drafts /data-structures/tries/` run (PowerShell, full run with Lighthouse, in the issue-107-tries worktree since that is where the draft lives): PASS, words=3274, code=15, fig=2, Lighthouse 100/100/100/100 across performance/accessibility/best-practices/seo. report.json confirms zero console errors, zero console warnings, zero broken links (6 external + 31 internal all resolve), mobileOverflowPx=0, exactly one <h1>, and zero placeholder/NEEDS_MARKUS markers (the byline renders as a plain 'Written by Computer Science Guide' organization link on this build, not a NEEDS_MARKUS(#n) marker, so the usually-expected placeholder failure does not apply here). Structure follows shape W cleanly and matches CONTENT_PLAN's outline for this row almost verbatim: the autocomplete problem stated abstractly -> a naive O(n x |p|) linear scan as the honest baseline -> the trie built and explained with Figure 1, immediately followed by an extend-the-code exercise (Trie.Remove) that reuses the same running example -> what the trie costs in memory, with a GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread measurement and a second exercise (predict-then-measure prefix-sharing, correctly shaped as measure-it) -> compressed/radix tries with Figure 2, grounded in a real citation (Linux fib_trie docs) rather than left hypothetical -> the sorted-array-plus-binary-search alternative built properly (lower-bound search, not a bare Array.BinarySearch call) -> a head-to-head benchmark from 500 to 200,000 words with real, non-fabricated numbers ('.NET 10.0.12 on Windows 11, build 22631, 16 logical processors') -> a decision section that names concrete conditions for reaching for a trie instead of just restating the headings. Nothing here is boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion'; each heading is specific to its content and the two exercises are correctly hidden (collapsed 'Show solution', question and program visible, output panel only inside the solution -- confirmed in mobile-light-part07/part08 and their dark equivalents) per the 'do not give away exercises' rule. Diagrams, which the writer could not check themselves: I inspected both figures directly in mobile-light-part03/part04, mobile-dark-part03/part04 (Figure 1) and mobile-light/dark-part08 (Figure 2), plus desktop-light-part02/part04, all at their actual rendered size. Figure 1 (viewBox 320x350, two stacked chains from a shared root, accent-colored nodes at r/e/l and o/t) is fully legible at 390px in both themes with no faded edge on either side -- it fits inside the 360-wide budget with margin to spare, labels are crisp d-mono text at readable size, and the accent/neutral node distinction (which nodes end a word) reads clearly in dark mode too, where the muted grey and teal accent both keep enough contrast against the near-black background. Figure 2 (viewBox 320x290, the compressed version with edge labels 'car'/'e'/'ful' on one side and 'do'/'t' on the other) renders with exactly five nodes as the caption promises, each edge label sitting directly above or beside its own edge rather than in a stranded legend, and the 'five nodes instead of eleven' annotation sits under the drawing per the phone rules rather than beside it. Both figures' source markup has no blank line inside the <figure> element, unique title/desc ids (trie-title/trie-desc, radix-title/radix-desc), and only d-* classes / CSS custom properties, no literal fill or stroke colors -- verified by reading the raw markdown directly. Neither figure becomes an awkwardly small island on the desktop screenshots; both sit centered in the content column at a sensible size. Code fencing matches WRITER_GUIDE/run-code.mjs conventions throughout: every csharp run id=... block is followed directly by a matching text output block (or, for the two long programs, the <details><summary>Full program</summary> collapsible pattern with the output block directly after the closing </details>, which renders correctly in the screenshots), timing and byte counts that vary run-to-run are wildcarded with [...] in the verified output blocks and only stated as prose or in a separate non-executed text block afterward, and the one illustrative (non-executed) code fence is absent -- everything that looks like C# is actually run. The one real, verifiable defect: in 'Measuring both, from 500 words to 200,000', both the wildcarded text output block and the real-numbers text block that follows it are formatted at roughly 48 characters wide (`{n,8} {arrayMB,9} {trieMB,9} {arrayus,9} {trieus,9}`), well past the ~40-character phone budget in WRITER_GUIDE.md section 7. Confirmed directly in mobile-light-part11 (and its dark equivalent): the visible portion of both blocks on a 390px screen shows only n, array MB, trie MB and array us -- the rightmost 'trie us' column (0.39 / 1.30 / 8.95 / 26.60 us) is entirely past the fade and never appears in either mobile screenshot. That column is specifically the number that backs the timing half of the article's central twin claim ('the sorted array used less memory and answered each query faster than the trie') -- the memory half (array MB vs trie MB) is fully visible and comparable without scrolling, but the time half is not: a mobile reader sees the array's own time-per-query figure but not the trie's, and has to scroll the output panel sideways to see the number the very next paragraph's prose is built on. This is exactly the case WRITER_GUIDE.md warns about ('if the last column is the evidence for a claim, it must not be the one that is cut off'). It does not sink the article -- the prose immediately after restates the qualitative conclusion in words, so no claim is left unsupported, and every other code and output block in the article is comfortably within budget -- but it is a real, specific mobile-readability defect in the article's own climactic measurement section, not a nit about phrasing.
